title: Metaphysics: Substance, Form, Matter and the Four Causes
subtitle: What is a thing, how does it change, and why does anything happen at all?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what Aristotle meant by substance and why individual things like this horse are the primary realities.
By the end you will be able to describe hylomorphism, the view that things are compounds of matter and form, using everyday examples.
By the end you will be able to use potentiality and actuality to explain how Aristotle answered Parmenides' denial of change.
By the end you will be able to name and apply the four causes (material, formal, efficient, final) to any object or event.
By the end you will be able to explain Aristotle's argument for an unmoved mover and what kind of 'god' it describes.
hook:
Pick up any ordinary object near you: a mug, a pen, a phone. Now ask four questions about it. What is it made of? What makes it *this kind* of thing rather than a lump of stuff? What brought it into being? And what is it *for*?

You probably answered all four without much effort. Clay. Its shape, with a handle and a hollow for liquid. A potter, or a factory. Holding hot drinks. Congratulations: you have just used one of the most influential ideas in the history of thought, Aristotle's **four causes**.

Yesterday we saw Aristotle build a toolkit for reasoning (Day 17). Today we see what he built with it: an answer to the deepest questions the Presocratics had raised. What is the world ultimately made of (Day 2)? How is change possible, if Parmenides was right that what-is cannot come from what-is-not (Day 5)? And is there a first source of all motion? Aristotle called this inquiry ‘first philosophy’. We call it **metaphysics**.

sections.heading: Being Qua Being: What 'Metaphysics' Means
sections.body:
Aristotle never wrote a book called *Metaphysics*. The title comes from ancient editors, probably in the first century BCE, who placed a group of his writings after (Greek *meta*) his works on nature (*ta physika*). *Ta meta ta physika* simply meant ‘the books after the physics’. By a happy accident the name stuck, and it fits: these books deal with questions that lie behind or beyond physics.

Aristotle himself called the subject **first philosophy**, wisdom, or sometimes theology. He describes it as the study of **being qua being**: not being *as* living (biology) or being *as* moving (physics) or being *as* countable (mathematics), but what it is for anything to *be* at all. It is the most general question possible.

His first insight is that ‘being’ is said in many ways. We say Socrates *is*, that he *is* pale, *is* five feet tall, *is* in the marketplace, *is* sitting. These are different kinds of being, and in his *Categories* (Day 17) Aristotle sorted them into a list of ten, including **substance**, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position and action. But they are not equal. Paleness, height and location all exist only *as features of* something else. There is no paleness floating around on its own. All the other categories depend on one: substance. So the question ‘what is being?’ becomes, Aristotle says, the question ‘what is substance?’

sections.heading: Substance: This Horse, This Person
sections.body:
In everyday English, ‘substance’ means stuff, like a sticky substance. Aristotle's Greek word, *ousia*, means something closer to ‘real being’ or ‘what a thing fundamentally is’. In the *Categories*, he gives a clear and down-to-earth answer: the primary substances are individual things, like **this man** or **this horse**.

Why? Because everything else depends on them. Colors, sizes and relationships are always the color, size or relationship *of* some individual thing. Even general kinds depend on individuals: if there were no individual horses at all, there would be no species ‘horse’. Aristotle calls species and genera (‘horse’, ‘animal’) **secondary substances**. They tell us *what* the primary substance is.

Notice how sharply this reverses Plato. For Plato (Day 11), the Form of Horse is the most real thing, and individual horses are pale copies. For Aristotle, the individual horse in the field is the most real thing, and the universal ‘horse’ exists only in such individuals (Day 16).

A substance has some distinctive marks. It is a *this*, an individual you can point to. It exists in its own right, not as a feature of something else. And it can remain the same thing while gaining and losing qualities: the same horse is first a foal and then grown, first healthy and then sick. This last point is the key to change. Something must persist through change for it to be change at all, rather than one thing vanishing and another appearing. Substance is that persisting something.

But what makes a substance the thing it is? Here Aristotle's thinking gets deeper, especially in Books VII and VIII (Zeta and Eta) of the *Metaphysics*, which are among the hardest texts in philosophy. His answer involves two ideas that go together: matter and form.

sections.heading: Hylomorphism: Matter and Form
sections.body:
Think of a bronze statue. What is it? In one sense, it is bronze: a certain amount of metal. In another sense, it is a statue of a runner, a particular shape and design. Neither alone is the statue. A lump of bronze is not yet a statue. A design in the sculptor's head is not yet a statue either. The statue is the bronze *shaped in a certain way*.

Aristotle generalizes this. Every physical substance is a compound of **matter** (Greek *hyle*) and **form** (Greek *morphe*, or *eidos*). The theory is therefore called **hylomorphism**. Matter is what a thing is made of: the potential stuff that can take on different forms. Form is the organization, structure or essence that makes it the specific kind of thing it is.

Two things make this idea much richer than it first sounds.

First, matter and form are relative. Bricks are matter for a house, but bricks themselves are clay given a form. Clay is matter for bricks, but clay is earth and water organized in a certain way. The house in turn could be matter for a street. Matter and form are not two kinds of stuff; they are two *roles* in an explanation.

Second, form is more than shape. For living things, form is the whole organization that lets the thing live and act as it does. The form of an eye is its power to see; a painted eye or a dead eye, Aristotle says, is an eye only in name. On Day 19 we will see him apply this to the **soul**, which he defines as the form of a living body. Your soul is not a ghost inside you, but the way your matter is organized so that you can grow, perceive and think.

Hylomorphism keeps what was right about Plato's Forms (that kinds and structures are real and knowable) while bringing them down to earth. Aristotle's forms do not live in a separate heaven. Apart from God, whom we meet below, a form exists only in the matter it organizes. The same word, *eidos*, now names something you can find by dissecting a fish.

sections.heading: Potentiality and Actuality: Solving Parmenides
sections.body:
Remember Parmenides' challenge (Day 5). Change would mean something coming to be from what is not. But what is not is nothing, and nothing comes from nothing. So change is impossible, and the senses deceive us. The Pluralists and Atomists (Days 6–7) tried to answer him by saying only arrangements change while the basic elements stay the same. Aristotle offers a subtler answer.

He distinguishes two ways of being. Something can be **actually** something (Greek *energeia* or *entelecheia*): what it is right now, fully realized. Or it can be **potentially** something (*dynamis*): what it is capable of becoming. An acorn is actually an acorn and potentially an oak tree. A block of marble is actually marble and potentially a statue. A student of French is actually a beginner and potentially fluent.

Now Parmenides' dilemma dissolves. When an acorn becomes an oak, the oak does not come from sheer nothing. It does not come from what *is* an oak, either, which would be no change. It comes from what is *potentially* an oak. Potentiality is a real way of being, in between ‘is’ and ‘is not’. Parmenides had only two options; Aristotle adds a third. In his *Physics*, he also explains that every change involves something that persists (the underlying subject, like the acorn's matter), a **privation** (the lack of the new form) and the form gained. The pale man becomes musical: the man persists, unmusicality is lost, musicality is gained.

Aristotle defines change itself, rather technically, as the actualization of what is potential, insofar as it is potential. The idea is that change is the process of a potential becoming real. Building is the actualizing of the buildable; learning is the actualizing of the learnable.

And crucially, Aristotle thinks actuality is prior to potentiality. A potential is always a potential *for* some actuality, and it takes something already actual to bring it about: an oak tree produces acorns, a teacher who already knows French teaches the student. Keep this principle in mind. It is the engine of his argument for God.

sections.heading: The Four Causes: Four Ways of Answering 'Why?'
sections.body:
Aristotle believed we only really know something when we grasp its **cause**. But his Greek word, *aition*, is broader than our word ‘cause’. It means any proper answer to a ‘why?’ question, any explanation. In *Physics* Book II, he argues that there are four basic kinds.

1. The **material cause**: what a thing is made of. The bronze of the statue; the bricks and timber of a house.
2. The **formal cause**: the form, structure or definition that makes it what it is. The shape of the statue; the design or plan of a house.
3. The **efficient cause**: the primary source of the change or rest, what brings it about. The sculptor (more precisely, the art of sculpture in the sculptor); the builder. A father is the efficient cause of a child.
4. The **final cause**: the end (Greek *telos*) or purpose, that for the sake of which something exists or happens. A house exists to shelter people and possessions; people take walks for the sake of health.

Take a simple example: a kitchen knife. Its material cause is steel. Its formal cause is its design: a sharp blade with a handle. Its efficient cause is the factory (or the smith) that made it. Its final cause is cutting food. Leave out any one of them and your explanation is incomplete.

Aristotle thought earlier philosophers had each grasped only part of this. The Milesians (Day 2) looked mainly for material causes: water, air, the apeiron. Empedocles' Love and Strife and Anaxagoras' Mind (Day 6) were attempts at efficient causes. Plato emphasized formal causes. But nobody, Aristotle thought, had properly recognized the **final cause**.

This is the most controversial of the four, because Aristotle applied it to nature, not only to human artifacts. Teeth grow sharp at the front for tearing food and broad at the back for grinding it. Plants send roots down for nourishment. Swallows build nests for their young. Aristotle saw purpose (*telos*) everywhere in living things, even though no one consciously designs them. Nature, he said, does nothing in vain. This view is called **teleology**, and it will be the main topic of Day 19. Modern science largely abandoned final causes in physics, starting with Bacon and Galileo (Day 41), but biologists still speak constantly of what organs are *for*.

sections.heading: The Unmoved Mover: Thought Thinking Itself
sections.body:
Aristotle's metaphysics ends, in Book XII (Lambda) of the *Metaphysics* and Book VIII of the *Physics*, with an argument for the existence of a divine being. It runs, roughly, like this.

1. Motion and change have always existed. Aristotle thought the universe had no beginning: time itself could not have started, since any first moment would need a moment before it.
2. The eternal, perfect motion of the universe is the steady circular movement of the heavens, which in Aristotle's astronomy were nested spheres carrying the stars and planets around the earth.
3. Everything that is moved is moved by something else. But the chain of movers cannot go back forever without a first source (compare the infinite regress problem of Day 16).
4. So there must be a first mover that is not itself moved: an **unmoved mover**.
5. This mover can have no potentiality at all, since anything with unrealized potential could change. It must be **pure actuality**, and therefore also immaterial, since matter is a source of potential.

How can something move other things without moving itself? Aristotle's answer is beautiful and strange. It moves them *as an object of love or desire moves*. A beautiful person can move admirers across a room without lifting a finger. In the same way, the heavens move in eternal circles out of a kind of longing to imitate the perfection of the unmoved mover. The unmoved mover is a final cause, not a push.

And what does it do? It cannot do anything that involves change. So its activity is the highest activity Aristotle knows: pure thinking. What does it think about? Only the best thing, which is itself. Its life is **thought thinking itself** (*noesis noeseos*), eternally and blissfully.

This is not the God of the Bible. Aristotle's god did not create the world, does not know or love individual human beings, answers no prayers, and gave no laws. Aristotle even suggested there might be many unmoved movers, one for each heavenly sphere, perhaps 47 or 55 of them. Yet this abstract god had enormous influence. Muslim, Jewish and Christian philosophers, including Avicenna, Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas (Days 32–35), adapted the argument from motion. The first of Aquinas' famous Five Ways (Day 35) is a version of it.

keyQuote.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a9 (a principle repeated across his biological works)

modernConnection.title: Form as Information: Aristotle, DNA and Software
modernConnection.body:
Aristotle's idea of form has had a surprising second life. In 1971 the Nobel Prize-winning biologist Max Delbrück published a playful essay suggesting that, if prizes could be awarded posthumously, Aristotle deserved one for recognizing the principle behind DNA. Delbrück's point was that Aristotle's ‘form’ is something like a plan or program that shapes matter into an organism without itself being a physical ingredient. A fertilized egg does not contain a tiny adult. It contains instructions, and those instructions organize food and water into a body. That sounds a lot like the genetic code.

The same idea appears in computing. Think of a song. It can exist as grooves in vinyl, magnetic patterns on tape, or electrical charges in your phone's memory. The matter is completely different each time, yet it is the *same song*, because the pattern, the form, is the same. Software can run on different hardware. Many philosophers of mind, as we will see on Day 84, think the mind is something like this: a pattern of organization, a ‘form’, that could in principle exist in different kinds of matter. This view, called functionalism, has often been compared to Aristotle's view of the soul.

The four causes also remain a useful thinking tool. Ask them of a pandemic, a smartphone or a social movement, and you will usually find that people arguing past each other are giving different kinds of explanation: one points to the material (the virus), another to the efficient (who spread it), another to the formal (the structure of the system), another to the final (what goals people pursued).

But the comparison has limits. DNA is itself matter, molecules made of atoms, not a non-physical form. And modern biology explains apparent purpose through natural selection, a blind process, not through natures striving toward their ends. Aristotle's insight about organization survives; his belief in purposes woven into nature remains hotly contested.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies the most basic nature of reality; for Aristotle, 'first philosophy', the study of being qua being. The name came from ancient editors.
vocabulary.example: Asking whether numbers really exist, or what makes something the same thing over time, is doing metaphysics.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's ousia: what fundamentally exists in its own right; primarily individual things like this man or this horse, on which qualities, quantities and relations depend.
vocabulary.example: For Aristotle, the horse in the field is a substance, while its brown color exists only as a feature of the horse.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's theory that physical substances are compounds of matter (hyle) and form (morphe), from the Greek words for each.
vocabulary.example: According to hylomorphism, a statue is not just bronze and not just a design, but bronze organized by a design.

vocabulary.definition: Two ways of being: what a thing is capable of becoming (potentiality, dynamis) and what it fully is now (actuality, energeia).
vocabulary.example: An acorn is actually an acorn and potentially an oak; growing is the actualization of that potentiality.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's four kinds of explanation: material (what it is made of), formal (its structure or essence), efficient (what brought it about) and final (what it is for).
vocabulary.example: The four causes of a house are its bricks, its design, its builder and its purpose of sheltering people.

vocabulary.definition: The end, goal or purpose (telos) for the sake of which a thing exists or a process happens.
vocabulary.example: Aristotle thought the final cause of sharp front teeth is tearing food.

vocabulary.definition: Explanation in terms of purposes or ends (from Greek telos); the view that natural things, especially living things, act for the sake of goals.
vocabulary.example: Saying 'the heart beats in order to pump blood' is a teleological explanation.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's eternal, immaterial first cause of motion, pure actuality with no potential, which moves the heavens as an object of love and whose activity is thought thinking itself.
vocabulary.example: Aquinas adapted Aristotle's unmoved mover into his first argument for the existence of God.

thinkingExercise.title: Four Causes of Something That Matters to You
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use Aristotle's four causes and his distinction between potentiality and actuality to analyze something in your own life.
steps: Choose something meaningful to you: an object (a gift, an instrument), an institution (your workplace, a team) or an event (a friendship, a career change).
Write out its four causes: what is it made of, what structure or form makes it what it is, what brought it about, and what is it for? Notice which cause was hardest to state.

Now consider yourself. Name one potentiality in you that is not yet actualized. What already-actual things (people, practices, resources) would be needed to bring it about, given Aristotle's principle that actuality comes first?

Finally, ask whether the 'final cause' you gave in step 2 is really in the thing itself, or whether it is something people project onto it. Write a short paragraph on where you think purpose comes from.

summary: Aristotle's 'first philosophy' studies being qua being; the title Metaphysics was added by later editors and meant 'after the physics'.
Of the ten categories, substance is primary: individual things like this horse exist in their own right, and qualities, quantities and kinds depend on them.
Hylomorphism says physical substances are compounds of matter and form; matter and form are relative roles, and form includes a living thing's whole organization.
Potentiality and actuality answer Parmenides: change is not from nothing but from what is potentially something, and actuality is prior to potentiality.
The four causes (material, formal, efficient, final) are four kinds of answer to 'why?'; Aristotle's final causes in nature (teleology) remain controversial.
The unmoved mover is pure actuality, moving the heavens as an object of love and eternally thinking itself; it is not a creator, but it deeply influenced later theology.

quiz.question: Where does the word 'metaphysics' come from?
options: Aristotle's own title for his greatest book
A term Plato invented for the study of the Forms
Ancient editors' label for the books placed after Aristotle's works on nature
A medieval Latin word meaning 'beyond the stars'
quiz.explanation: Ta meta ta physika meant 'the books after the physics'. Aristotle called the subject first philosophy.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle's Categories, what are the primary substances?
options: Individual things, such as this man or this horse
The Forms, such as Beauty itself
The four elements: earth, water, air and fire
Qualities such as color and size
quiz.explanation: Individuals are primary because everything else, including qualities and species, depends on them for its existence.

quiz.question: For Aristotle, matter and form are two separate kinds of stuff that can each exist on their own in ordinary physical objects.
quiz.explanation: Matter and form are two aspects or roles within a single substance. In physical things, form exists only in the matter it organizes, and what counts as matter is relative (bricks are matter for a house but formed clay themselves).

quiz.question: How does the distinction between potentiality and actuality answer Parmenides?
options: It shows that change is an illusion, as Parmenides claimed
It proves that atoms move through a void
It shows that everything is made of a single element
It shows that change comes not from sheer nothing but from what is potentially something
quiz.explanation: Parmenides allowed only 'is' and 'is not'. Aristotle adds potential being, so the oak comes from what is potentially an oak, not from nothing.

quiz.question: In explaining a violin, which is its formal cause?
options: The wood and strings
The luthier who built it
Its design and structure as a stringed instrument of a particular shape
Making music
quiz.explanation: The formal cause is the structure or definition. The wood is the material cause, the maker the efficient cause, and making music the final cause.

quiz.question: Which question does the final cause answer?
options: What is it made of?
What is it for?
Who made it?
When did it begin?
quiz.explanation: The final cause is the telos, the purpose or end for the sake of which something exists or happens.

quiz.question: Aristotle's unmoved mover moves the heavens by pushing them, like a hand pushing a wheel.
quiz.explanation: It moves them as an object of love or desire moves, without itself moving. It is a final cause, not a mechanical push.

quiz.question: Which modern idea is closest to Aristotle's notion of form?
options: The total weight of the atoms in an object
The chemical elements listed in the periodic table
A pattern of organization, like a song that can be stored on vinyl or in digital memory
The Big Bang as the first event in time
quiz.explanation: Form is the organization that makes matter into a particular kind of thing; the same pattern can be realized in different materials, as with a song or software.

quiz.question: Which of the following is TRUE of Aristotle's unmoved mover?
options: It created the universe at a moment in time
It is pure actuality and its activity is thought thinking itself
It answers prayers and gives moral laws
It is made of the finest kind of matter, called aether
quiz.explanation: The unmoved mover has no potentiality and is immaterial; it thinks only of itself. Aristotle believed the universe had no beginning, so it is not a creator.

quiz.question: Aristotle thought final causes apply not only to human-made objects but also to natural things like teeth and plant roots.
quiz.explanation: This is his teleology: nature does nothing in vain, and living things have parts that exist for the sake of ends, even though no one designed them.

goDeeper.body:
The central books of the *Metaphysics* (VII–IX, Zeta, Eta and Theta) contain one of philosophy's great unsolved puzzles. In the *Categories*, primary substance is the individual: this horse. But in *Metaphysics* Zeta, Aristotle asks what makes this horse a substance, and he seems to conclude that the primary substance is the *form*, the essence of the thing. Yet he also holds that substance is individual and that knowledge is of universals. So is form individual (Socrates' own form, different from Callias' form) or universal (the same human form in both)? Scholars have argued about this for decades. Michael Frede and Günther Patzig defended individual forms; others, such as Michael Loux, defend a universal reading. The answer matters for understanding how Aristotle meant to improve on Plato.

Another debate concerns the four causes. Are they really four separate causes, or, as Aristotle hints, do formal, efficient and final causes often coincide? In living things, the form of a human is also what a human develops toward (final cause), and it is a human father who generates a child (efficient cause). The organism's form, its goal and its source turn out to be the same thing seen from different angles.

Finally, how should we read Book Lambda? Some take the unmoved mover as the crown of Aristotle's system, the being that explains why there is order at all. Others see it as an awkward add-on to an otherwise naturalistic philosophy. Medieval thinkers from Avicenna to Aquinas used it to build bridges between Greek philosophy and monotheism (Days 32–35), while modern physics, with Newton's principle of inertia, removed the need for anything to keep the heavens moving.

readings.title: Physics, Book II
readings.author: Aristotle (trans. R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, in The Complete Works of Aristotle, ed. Jonathan Barnes)
readings.note: Chapters 3 and 7 set out the four causes; chapter 8 defends final causes in nature against the idea that everything happens by necessity or chance.

readings.title: Metaphysics, Book XII (Lambda), chapters 6–9
readings.author: Aristotle (trans. W. D. Ross)
readings.note: Short, dense and extraordinary: the argument for the unmoved mover and the description of its life as thought thinking itself.

readings.title: Aristotle: The Desire to Understand
readings.author: Jonathan Lear
readings.note: A beautifully written introduction that makes Aristotle's metaphysics feel like a living answer to real puzzles.

readings.title: Aristotle
readings.author: Christopher Shields
readings.note: A clear, thorough guide to Aristotle's metaphysics, including the debates about substance and form.

questions: Is it legitimate to ask what natural things are 'for', or should final causes be reserved for human-made objects and intentions?
If all the matter in your body is gradually replaced (remember Heraclitus on Day 4), are you still the same substance? What would Aristotle say keeps you the same?
Does Aristotle's argument for an unmoved mover still work if the universe had a beginning, or if it never needed anything to keep it moving?
